source_agency: Council of the District of Columbia
methodology: Hand-verified inventory of enacted traffic-safety laws and one codified fund that map to Vision Zero delivery questions. Each record summarizes legal requirements only; implementation status and compliance claims require separate source review.
caveats: This file is not legal advice.
Dollar figures from press coverage are intentionally excluded until verified against OCFO, OAG, court, or budget primary sources.
Delivery pointers are tracking prompts, not findings that an agency is compliant or non-compliant.

laws.title: Vision Zero Enhancement Omnibus Amendment Act of 2020
laws.summary: Comprehensive Vision Zero package requiring safety reporting, sidewalk and crosswalk protections, protected bike lane and multimodal-priority triggers during reconstruction, local and collector street speed limits of 20 mph or less, and specified automated-enforcement infrastructure.
requirements: DDOT must submit a Vision Zero infrastructure progress report on the District's top 15 most dangerous corridors for pedestrians and cyclists.
The corridor report must explain how proposed projects increase safety, improve equitable access to public transportation, support mode-share goals, and decrease motor-vehicle speeds.
Local and collector streets must have a speed limit of 20 mph or less.
Right turns on red must be prohibited near specified schools, parks, libraries, playgrounds, Metrorail station entrances, or bike-lane intersections unless DDOT publishes a safety explanation.

delivery_pointers.label: Compare statutory top-15 corridor reporting against the High Injury Network
delivery_pointers.note: The current hotspot data ranks DDOT High Injury Network corridors by KSI and can seed an audit of whether the statutory corridor reporting is findable.

delivery_pointers.label: Use the ANC brief for corridor-specific asks
delivery_pointers.note: The law's reporting standard gives ANCs a concrete question: what safety project is promised for this corridor, and how does it reduce speed or increase safe access?

laws.title: Safer Streets Amendment Act of 2022
laws.summary: Updates bicycle and intersection rules, including bicycle stop-as-yield provisions, bicycle right-on-red where allowed, and a motor-vehicle right-on-red restriction framework.
requirements: A rider approaching a stop sign may proceed through the intersection at a safe speed after yielding when required by law.
A rider may make a right turn at a steady red after stopping, checking for immediate hazards, and yielding to pedestrians and lawful traffic.
Motor-vehicle right turns on red are restricted unless DDOT determines a turn improves safety or traffic flow and posts the required sign.
DDOT must publish and maintain a list of intersections where right turns on red are allowed.

delivery_pointers.label: Track right-on-red exceptions
delivery_pointers.note: Pair crash records near schools, stations, parks, and bike lanes with DDOT's published exception list before making any compliance claim.

laws.title: Safe Streets for Students Amendment Act of 2022
laws.summary: Builds a school-zone safety program: safe-passage staffing and grants, a Safe Routes to School program, a School Streets pilot, a multi-year Safe Streets for Students Master Plan, and lower school-zone speed limits with doubled fines.
requirements: DDOT must operate a Safe Routes to School Program and produce school safety action plans for at least 25 schools per school year.
A School Streets Pilot Program must run at a minimum of one school per ward.
A Safe Streets for Students Master Plan must be produced and refreshed on a multi-year cycle.
School zones must carry a 15 mph speed limit between 6:00 a.m. and 7:00 p.m., with doubled fines for moving violations in school zones.

delivery_pointers.label: Check school-zone fixes against the crash map
delivery_pointers.note: The law promises action plans for at least 25 schools a year; pair the school list with nearby crash records before claiming a given school zone is treated.

laws.title: Strengthening Traffic Enforcement, Education, and Responsibility Amendment Act of 2024
laws.summary: Creates stronger tools for repeat dangerous driving, including booting and towing eligibility, safe-driving education, civil enforcement authority, and an Intelligent Speed Assistance program for qualifying convictions.
requirements: Vehicles with 10 or more points in a 6-month period can become booting- and towing-eligible.
DMV must establish a safe-driving course tied to fine reductions within statutory limits.
The District gains authority to pursue certain unpaid moving-violation debts through civil actions.
DMV must operate an Intelligent Speed Assistance program for people whose reinstatement conditions require enrollment.

delivery_pointers.label: Keep enforcement claims separate from engineering recommendations
delivery_pointers.note: Use STEER as legal authority context, not as a substitute for street-design fixes where the crash pattern points to speed management or infrastructure.

laws.title: Automated Traffic Enforcement System Revenue Designation Amendment Act of 2022
laws.status: enacted; fiscal applicability tied to approved budget and financial plan
laws.summary: Specifies priority uses for the Vision Zero Enhancement Omnibus Amendment Act Implementation Fund, connecting automated-enforcement revenue to implementation of street-safety laws and pedestrian/bicycle safety work.
requirements: Fund money is prioritized for implementing specified sections of the Vision Zero Enhancement Omnibus Amendment Act of 2020.
Fund money is also prioritized for implementing the Safer Streets Amendment Act of 2022 and Safe Streets for Students provisions.
Remaining eligible uses include pedestrian and bicycle safety, education, engineering, enforcement, traffic calming, and safe routes.

delivery_pointers.label: Audit revenue-to-safety claims only from budget primary sources
delivery_pointers.note: Press-reported camera revenue figures are useful leads, but the site should wait for OCFO or budget source records before displaying dollar totals.

laws.title: Vision Zero Pedestrian and Bicycle Safety Fund
laws.summary: A special fund for pedestrian and bicycle safety that receives specified automated-enforcement fines and DMV fees, and may be used only for safety and quality improvements including education, engineering, enforcement, traffic calming, and safe routes.
requirements: $500,000 per fiscal year from automated traffic enforcement fines is deposited in the fund.
Specified DMV fees are deposited in the fund.
The fund must be used solely to enhance pedestrian and bicycle transportation safety and quality.

delivery_pointers.label: Treat this as a funding trail, not a spending finding
delivery_pointers.note: The code creates the fund and allowed uses; actual annual deposits and expenditures need budget and financial records.
